title: ProofDebt: When Does Memory Improve Continual Software Repair?
content: Coding agents are increasingly expected to work on the same repository over time, yet most evaluations treat every issue as a fresh start. This makes a basic question hard to answer: when should memory help? We introduce PROOFDEBT, a continual-repair protocol whose memory is built from native-test outcomes, changed files, dependency links, and patch status rather than self-written summaries. A primary campaign contains 891 repair attempts across 11 three-step ChainSWE chains and three model families. Across 1,188 token-matched later-step attempts, PROOFDEBT improves success over reset by 6.6 percentage points, but the average hides an important difference between tasks. Two coders independently audit all 22 later-step tasks and agree on 19 of 22 information-need labels before adjudication (86.4%; unweighted Cohen’s κ = 0.77). Their consensus audit identifies seven tasks where the correct repair genuinely needs information from an earlier repair. On these tasks, reset succeeds on 14.3% of attempts, PROOFDEBT on 60.3%, and an oracle memory condition on 82.5%. On the other 15 tasks, the three conditions remain within 4.5 points. A trace audit shows that practical ledgers usually contain the right obligation but often fail to present it as something the model must preserve. These results suggest that continual-agent evaluations should measure whether a task offers a real opportunity for memory before averaging memory effects.
